passages.happening:
Amaziah reigns twenty-nine years. ‘And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, but not wholeheartedly’ (verse 2). He executes the servants who murdered his father, but not their sons, ‘according to what is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses’ (verse 4).

He hires a hundred thousand soldiers from Israel for a hundred talents of silver (verse 6). A man of God tells him, “O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you, for the LORD is not with Israel” (verse 7). Amaziah asks about the money already paid, and the man of God answers, “The LORD is able to give you much more than this” (verse 9). Amaziah sends the hired troops home, and they leave angry (verse 10). He defeats the men of Seir in the Valley of Salt (verse 11). The verse that follows tells of captives killed by Judah's army (verse 12). The dismissed Israelite troops raid the towns of Judah (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Joash's reign ended with a murdered prophet and an assassinated king. His son begins by setting things right, but the opening verdict hangs over everything: right, but not wholeheartedly, shalem, the undivided heart David prayed for. The chapter shows what a divided heart looks like: Amaziah can obey a prophet when it costs money, yet cannot resist the gods of a people he has just defeated. Early faithfulness followed by pride and decline is becoming a habit in Judah's kings.

He reigned about 796 to 767 BC; because verse 25 says he lived fifteen years after Jehoash of Israel died, many think Uzziah ruled beside him for part of that time. Second Kings 14 tells the victory over Edom and the war with Jehoash; Chronicles adds the hired troops, the two prophets and the worship of Edom's gods. Edom had rebelled under Jehoram. Hiring soldiers was common, and a hundred talents was a huge sum. The prophet's objection is to relying on Israel, which had broken with the temple and David's line.

Verse 12 reports the killing of captives without praise. Nothing says God commanded it, and the chapter goes straight on to condemn Amaziah. Killing prisoners was common in ancient war; some read the act as part of the portrait of a king whom success was already corrupting. The reader is not invited to celebrate it, and these notes do not dwell on it.
passages.later: Amaziah's mercy to the murderers' sons follows the law: ‘Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin’ (Deuteronomy 24:16).
passages.asks: Amaziah let go of a hundred talents because God was able to give him more. Ask what you are holding onto only because you have already paid for it. And ask where your obedience is real but not wholehearted.

passages.t: The gods of Edom, and a thistle's challenge
passages.happening:
‘When Amaziah returned from the slaughter of the Edomites, he brought back the gods of the Seirites, set them up as his own gods, bowed before them, and burned sacrifices to them’ (verse 14). God sends a prophet: “Why have you sought this people’s gods, which could not deliver them from your hand?” (verse 15). The king cuts him off, “Have we made you the counselor to the king?” (verse 16), and the prophet says, “I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not heeded my advice” (verse 16).

Amaziah takes counsel and challenges Jehoash king of Israel (verse 17). Jehoash answers with a fable of a thistle that asked a cedar for its daughter, and a wild beast that trampled the thistle (verse 18). Amaziah will not listen. Judah is routed at Beth-shemesh, Jehoash breaks down part of Jerusalem's wall and takes the temple's gold and silver and hostages (verses 21-24). ‘From the time that Amaziah turned from following the LORD, a conspiracy was formed against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But men were sent after him to Lachish, and they killed him there’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Worshiping a defeated people's gods looks senseless, but it had an ancient logic. Conquerors often carried off the images of conquered gods, to display victory or to win their favor. The prophet exposes the absurdity in one question: why seek gods that could not save their own people? The word sought is darash, the Chronicler's word for true worship, turned against the king.

The chapter turns on counsel. The root for advise, yaats, runs through verses 16 and 17: Amaziah asks whether the prophet has been made the king's counselor, the prophet says God has counseled to destroy him because he would not heed counsel, and Amaziah then takes counsel elsewhere and goes to war. The man who will not hear God's counsel finds other counsel that destroys him. Verse 20 names the hidden cause: his refusal to listen came from God, because Judah had sought the gods of Edom.

Jehoash, grandson of Jehu, answers with a fable, a short plant-and-animal story used to mock a rival, like Jotham's fable of the trees in Judges. Beth-shemesh lay in the Sorek valley west of Jerusalem, and Lachish was Judah's great fortress in the lowlands.
passages.later: In Jotham's fable in Judges the thornbush says, ‘But if not, may fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon’ (Judges 9:15).
passages.hard:
How should a reader understand the killing of ten thousand captives in verse 12?

The text reports this atrocity without praise; nothing says God commanded it, and the chapter immediately condemns Amaziah for what he did after the battle. Chronicles often records the brutal conduct of war in the ancient Near East, where killing prisoners was common, without endorsing it. Some readers see the act as part of the portrait of a king whose success was already corrupting him. Others note that large numbers in Chronicles may be stylized or may count military units rather than individuals, a debated point. Either way the chapter's verdict falls on the king's pride and idolatry, and the reader is not invited to celebrate the slaughter.
passages.asks: Amaziah silenced the prophet with a question about who had made him counselor. Ask whose counsel you have refused because it came from someone you did not think had standing to give it. And ask what gods of the people around you you have carried home after a success.
